title: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to an Average Salary: A 38-Hour Week Guide
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to an average salary using a 38-hour week, 52-week year. Includes fortnightly pay, tax, super, and Fair Work rates.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, annual gross pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 38 then by 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: What is the formula to convert hourly rate to annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52. For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super. If you work different hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. The result assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my annual salary?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. If you are a casual employee, your annual salary estimate should use the loaded rate. On the timesheet tool, you can check a box to add 25% casual loading to your base rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool adds it automatically.

faqs.q: How are tax and super calculated from my annual salary?
faqs.a: Tax is based on the 2026–27 resident tax scale: nil up to $18,200, then 15% to $45,000, 30% to $135,000, 37% to $190,000, and 45% above that. Medicare levy is generally 2%. Super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid on top of your salary, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. The estimate here does not include HELP repayments, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Annual Salary from Your Hourly Rate

When you’re paid by the hour, it’s helpful to know what that adds up to over a year. Whether you’re comparing a salary offer or planning your budget, converting your hourly rate to an **average salary** gives you a clear picture. This guide explains the standard method using a 38-hour week, a fortnight, and a 52-week year, and covers the key differences between minimum wage, award rates, casual loading, super, and tax.

### The Basic Formula

The core calculation is simple: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 (the number of weeks in a year). For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, if your hourly rate is $30.00, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This is your pay before tax and super. The formula assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. If your weekly hours differ, adjust the 38 accordingly.

### The Fortnightly View

Many Australian employers pay fortnightly. To find your gross fortnightly pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the example above, weekly pay is $30 × 38 = $1,140, so fortnightly pay is $1,140 × 2 = $2,280. This can help you match your budget to your pay cycle.

### National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The **National Minimum Wage** is set by the Fair Work Commission. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. For casual employees, the minimum casual rate is $33.05 per hour, which includes a 25% casual loading. However, most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates for their industry or role. These award rates vary by classification and may include penalty rates, allowances, and overtime. Always check your specific award via the Fair Work Ombudsman’s [pay guides](/blog) or [reference tables](/data). The **average salary** figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) are broader benchmarks, not your job’s median.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Super guarantee is a compulsory contribution your employer must pay into your super fund. From 1 July 2026, the rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid **on top** of your salary. It does not come out of your hourly rate. For the example above, annual super would be 12% of $59,280 = $7,113.60, but only up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is not included in your take-home pay; it’s an extra retirement benefit.

### Tax Considerations

Your gross annual pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) applies a progressive tax scale for residents in 2026–27:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. The tax estimate here uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool to see an estimate after tax and Medicare.

### Average Salary Benchmarks

The ABS Average Weekly Earnings (May 2026) report shows:
- Full-time adult ordinary time earnings: $2,083.70 per week
- All employees total earnings (including part-time): $1,579.20 per week

These are **averages** across all industries and states, not the median for your specific job. For a more tailored comparison, look at industry or occupation averages from the ABS or your award. The [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page can help you understand these benchmarks.

### Using the Timesheet Tool

The [timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your base hourly rate and see the annual, fortnightly, and weekly equivalents. If you are a casual employee, check the box to add 25% casual loading on top. **Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – the tool adds it for you. The result includes an estimate of super (12% on top) and tax using the 2026–27 resident scale. Remember, this is an estimate, not a determination of your actual pay or tax.

### Important Notes

This conversion assumes a consistent 38-hour week, 52 weeks per year. It does not account for unpaid leave, public holidays, or overtime. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold, but does not deduct HELP, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Always consult the Fair Work Ombudsman for your award and the ATO for your personal tax situation.
